title: Prefetch Coalescing and Eviction Safety Review with Novus Labs
summary: SE-led deep dive on prefetch coalescing heuristics, eviction safety for shared KV cache, multi-tenant collision mitigation, and on-prem/VPC constraints. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot: small benchmark with 3 workload patterns, verify hit-rate improvements and no tenant leakage, share security appendix and eviction logs access.
action_items: Maya - produce prefetch simulation script and sample results by 2026-07-01
Novus (Samir) - provide representative API traffic traces (anonymized) by 2026-06-29
Alex - share security appendix + SOC2 checklist and KMS integration notes by 2026-06-26
Jordan - run initial 3-variant micro-benchmark on Dedicated equivalent and share metrics by 2026-07-03
next_steps: Schedule pilot kickoff (2-week) after Novus sends traces
Redwood to provide a pre-configured pilot profile (prefetch off/on/coalesce)
Exchange dataset sampling notes and acceptable PII redaction process
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-24 16:00 PDT | Duration: 55 minutes | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Solutions Eng) -- Priya Kapoor (Novus CTO), Samir Patel (Novus Platform Eng), Elena Morales (Novus Security), Liam O'Connor (Novus SRE)
---
00:00:03 Alex Chen: okay great everyone thanks for joining, uh we are gonna focus on prefetch coalescing and eviction safety today, quick run of the agenda, myself and Maya will lead then Jordan will walk through a brief micro-benchmark, Priya over to you for constraints up front
00:00:18 Priya Kapoor: thanks Alex yeah quick context, Novus is moving more inference to private clusters, latency SLOs at 120 ms p95, we have heavy multi-tenant traffic (internal prod + external partners), some tenants have spiky conversational loads, and we want to maximize kv cache hit rate without risking cross-tenant leakage
00:00:36 Maya Singh: absolutely that's exactly the tradeoff we wanted to highlight. we'll cover keying, coalescing heuristics, grace windows on eviction, and how quantization changes signature stability
00:00:50 Samir Patel: one ask up front, we cannot have any possibility of returning cached content from a different tenant even if the prompt keys match, so namespace isolation is non-negotiable. also on-prem means limited ability for us to share raw traffic, we can send anonymized traces
00:01:06 Alex Chen: understood, good call-out. we'll propose tenant namespacing and HMAC keying so the cache keys are tenant-bound. Maya, can you open on key construction?
00:01:15 Maya Singh: sure. so canonical key is a hash over: tenant-id, model-id+version, normalized prompt prefix, tokenizer-decoded normalize, and a small runtime fingerprint (temperature, stop tokens). we then HMAC that with tenant-specific secret when in private mode or with workspace-scoped key in hosted. the difference for on-prem/vpc is the key provisioning step - KMS or local HSM integration
00:01:42 Priya Kapoor: does that add CPU overhead at inference path? we care about per-request CPU on our edge routers
00:01:49 Maya Singh: it's cheap, hmac-sha256 on the short key is negligible compared to tokenization and model infer. we do precompute keys at the router tier for batches when possible. that said the expensive part can be normalization - canonicalizing prompts and removing volatile bits
00:02:09 Liam O'Connor: normalization is tricky for us, our prompts sometimes include timestamps, ephemeral ids, json payloads that vary. what's the recommended approach?
:02:20 Jordan Lee: we often advise a layered normalization: strip high-entropy fields (regex for timestamps/uuids), canonicalize whitespacing, and optionally produce a semantic fingerprint using a small embed model to capture paraphrases for longer prefixes. that embedding step is optional and we call it semantic shingling
00:02:40 Samir Patel: embedding for keying sounds costly. won't that create a new bottleneck?
00:02:46 Maya Singh: yes there's cost. so we recommended a hybrid: exact-hash for small prefixes and semantic fingerprinting only for requests that fall below a certain exact-hash hit threshold. that's where prefetch coalescing comes in
00:02:58 Alex Chen: let me explain coalescing quickly: if multiple in-flight requests share the same canonical key within a small time window, we coalesce to a single backend generation and fan-out responses. prefetch coalescing extends that by proactively issuing a 'prefetch' request for predicted next-prefixes for a given session or tenant hotset. the heuristics determine when to prefetch to avoid wasted cycles
00:03:23 Priya Kapoor: and how do you stop prefetch from polluting the cache and impacting eviction for other tenants? we saw that in other systems where prefetch fills the hotset with non-useful items
00:03:33 Maya Singh: good question. we use three mechanisms: 1) prefetch entries are written with a lower permanence score (shorter TTL + mem-tier tagging), 2) eviction respects tenant quotas so a tenant's prefetches can't evict another tenant's items, and 3) prefetch bloom filter: we mark entries as 'speculative' and they are first-class but lower priority for serving in strict SLO contexts
00:03:56 Elena Morales: marking speculative entries in logs is okay, we need clear auditable flags so security can trace if a speculative entry was served to a tenant incorrectly. we also need to ensure HMAC keys are rotated and logs show tenant-id at every step
00:04:09 Maya Singh: yes, we can surface a speculative flag in the tracing logs and provide a per-tenant eviction and access audit. for VPC/on-prem deployment we support local log sinks and can redact PII at the ingestion window
00:04:25 Samir Patel: how about eviction policy specifics? we currently use LRU with a per-tenant soft quota but that's causing cascades when one tenant spikes
00:04:34 Maya Singh: for spike isolation we recommend a multi-tier eviction: hotset (frequent hits), warmset (recent), speculative (prefetch), and an adaptive grace window. tenants get a guaranteed soft memory cap and an overflow buffer that decays. when overflow triggers, the runtime preferentially evicts speculative then warm then hot within that tenant before touching other tenants' hot items
00:04:58 Priya Kapoor: what's the grace window? if you evict an item too early we lose the session context and p95 balloons
00:05:06 Jordan Lee: grace window is workload dependent; we typically simulate with trace replay. in our prior customers, a 30-90s grace window for hot conversational prefixes gave best p95 without eating memory. for long-running sessions, we recommend sticky local cache pins for the session leader with explicit TTL hints from the app layer
00:05:29 Liam O'Connor: any concerns about quantization affecting key stability? we quantize models heavily and sometimes outputs drift slightly between formats
00:05:38 Maya Singh: quantization affects output generation but not the input prefix key; however it can affect whether two prefixes that look identical to a human will produce similar tokenization results if tokenizers differ across quantized runtime builds. we ensure keying uses canonical tokenizer (same vocab, tokenizer versions) and we include model build-id in the key string so caches don't collide across quantization variants
00:06:02 Samir Patel: interesting, so model build id must be deterministic and pinned in our deploys. what about batch versus latency tradeoff — prefetch improves throughput but could harm p95 if prefetch contention starves live requests
00:06:15 Maya Singh: that's why we throttle prefetch based on queue depth and active latency SLOs. prefetch jobs are lower priority and get CPU only when load is below a threshold. also prefetch coalescing groups prefetches for multiple sessions to amortize cost
00:06:28 Priya Kapoor: can Redwood run a pilot in our VPC setup? we have strict network egress and KMS in-house
00:06:36 Alex Chen: yes, we support private mode. for pilot we can operate fully within your VPC with our control plane disabled if you prefer. we'll use your KMS for HMAC key provisioning. Jordan will talk about the benchmark shape we propose
00:06:50 Jordan Lee: thanks. slide: micro-benchmark plan. three workload shapes: 1) bursty chat (short prefixes, many continuations), 2) template-based transactional (prompts with small variable fields), 3) long-context synthesis (long prefixes). we'll replay sampled traces with/without prefetch and with different coalescing windows (100ms, 500ms, 1s) and measure hit-rate, p95, and extra compute used
00:07:18 Samir Patel: how do you measure "extra compute"? are you capturing token generation cost or whole VM CPU?
00:07:24 Jordan Lee: both. we capture model GPU time (tokens/sec), orchestration CPU for keying and prefetch, and net effect on latency p95. we also capture prefetch waste metric: ratio of prefetches never used within TTL
00:07:38 Elena Morales: for security please include a step to show we never serve a cache entry originating from another tenant. include audit traces for each serve event
00:07:47 Maya Singh: yes audit traces are part of the benchmark output. each serve event includes key-id, tenant-hmac prefix, cache-tag (hot/warm/spec), and verification that tenant-id matched the request. we can run a breach simulation where we intentionally scramble tenant-hmac to verify we never serve cross-tenant data
00:08:03 Priya Kapoor: that would be useful. also compliance wants to see retention TTLs and ability to force purge for a tenant
00:08:11 Alex Chen: we have APIs to purge per-tenant or per-key patterns, and in private mode the purge commands can be routed to your local operator. we'll include that in the appendix we share
00:08:23 Samir Patel: on the coalescing window numbers, do you have guidance for us given 120ms p95 target? we'd want coalescing to not add 50ms to p95
00:08:33 Maya Singh: with a 120ms SLO, we typically keep coalescing window sub-50ms for live paths; prefetch windows can be longer because it's asynchronous. coalescing is mostly used at the router to avoid duplicate requests within the same batch tick. if you have a fast edge, you can push coalescing to 20-30ms safely
00:08:48 Liam O'Connor: are there failure modes where coalescing increases tail latencies due to lock contention?
00:08:53 Jordan Lee: yes if implemented with global locks. Redwood uses lock-free KV indices and optimistic concurrency for in-flight coalescing: the first request wins and others attach to the in-flight promise, so we avoid lock queue head-of-line blocking. still, pathological storms can cause head requests to balloon so we have back-pressure controls
00:09:12 Priya Kapoor: let's talk numbers — what hit-rate lift did customers see with prefetch?
00:09:18 Maya Singh: depends heavily on workload. for bursty chat we saw hit-rate go from 12% -> 48% in a customer with stable templates and session behavior. for template transactional workloads it was smaller but more predictable, 25% -> 40%. the cost was ~10-18% extra model compute due to prefetch waste which we offset with batch savings in other layers
00:09:39 Samir Patel: 10-18% extra compute is material for us; can you reduce that with better prediction?
00:09:45 Maya Singh: yes prediction improves with session-level heuristics and ephemeral ML models that predict continuation probability. for pilot we can enable a conservative prefetch policy (only when continuation probability > 0.8) to keep waste under 5%
00:09:58 Alex Chen: also quantization/throughput improvements on Dedicated can reduce net cost so even with a small prefetch overhead unit cost goes down
00:10:07 Priya Kapoor: we need to decide what we want the pilot to measure: hit-rate, p95, prefetch waste, cross-tenant leakage attempts. anything else?
00:10:15 Elena Morales: also prove key rotation/rotation audit and purging, compliance playback of logs for 30 days.
00:10:22 Liam O'Connor: include eviction cascade simulation — trigger tenant spike and observe neighbor tenants' hit-rate
00:10:28 Jordan Lee: agreed. we'll include a synthetic spike test in the benchmark plan.
00:10:34 Maya Singh: operational notes: for on-prem we ship a small prefetch controller that can be tuned (prefetch concurrency, TTL multiplier for speculative), and we expose telemetry: per-tenant hit-rate, speculative ratio, eviction rate, prefetch waste ratio, coalescing hit ratio
00:10:51 Samir Patel: can we get raw eviction logs? we want to correlate with our app-level errors; retention of logs is a compliance question
00:10:58 Alex Chen: yes you can configure retention and local sinks. for pilot we can keep logs for 30 days and redact PII.
00:11:07 Priya Kapoor: anything on legal/audit — do you support subprocessor disclosure for any hosted bits?
00:11:13 Alex Chen: for private mode we minimize third-party subprocessors; we will share the subprocessor list and can sign a narrow DPA addendum for the pilot
00:11:23 Elena Morales: make sure we get SOC2 docs and architecture diagram with network boundaries
00:11:28 Alex Chen: will do. action items recap in a moment.
00:11:33 Jordan Lee: a couple more technical edge cases: what if tokenization changes across a minor model update and keys start missing? we recommend model-version pinning for cache warmness and a rolling rekey + rehydration process where we invalidate and optionally warm hot prefixes after a model swap
00:11:51 Maya Singh: optionally we can run a small compatibility check in the deployment pipeline to detect tokenizer diffs (vocab ids mismatch) before we flip. if mismatch, we run full cache flush for that model id.
00:12:05 Priya Kapoor: okay that helps.
00:12:08 Alex Chen: quick recap of decisions and next steps?
00:12:12 Priya Kapoor: we want the 2-week pilot, we'll send anonymized traces by Monday, want the breach simulation included, need security appendix and SOC2, plus purge API details
00:12:23 Alex Chen: perfect. Maya/Jordan you'll run the prefetch sim and propose pilot profile. we'll share the appendix and schedule kickoff when traces arrive.
00:12:32 Maya Singh: noted. we'll also include the speculative flag in logs and an example of the audit trace format.
00:12:38 Samir Patel: any follow-ups on pricing for Dedicated pilot?
00:12:42 Alex Chen: pricing will be a simple pilot rate for the 2-week footprint; I'll follow up with a pilot quote via email.
00:12:49 Elena Morales: please send the SOC2 and subprocessor info to security@novuslabs.com
00:12:54 Alex Chen: will do.
00:12:57 Priya Kapoor: thanks all, I have to jump but Samir and Elena will stay for any deeper follow-ups.
00:13:03 Alex Chen: thanks Priya. we'll put notes in calendar and send the materials.
00:13:08 [call transitions to technical sandbox discussion and screen share]
00:13:35 Jordan Lee: starting benchmark demo, replaying trace A with prefetch off - p95 baseline 118ms, hit-rate 14%...
00:14:05 Maya Singh: note that clock skew in these synthetic runs makes small p95 deltas noisy, focal points are hit-rate and prefetch waste
00:14:35 Jordan Lee: replay with prefetch conservative (prob>0.8) coalesce 100ms: hit-rate up to 33%, p95 stable at 122ms, prefetch waste 4.8%
00:15:10 Samir Patel: what's causing p95 small bump?
00:15:14 Jordan Lee: slight scheduling jitter from prefetch threads but still within noise; with stricter priority we can avoid that.
00:15:26 Jordan Lee: replay with aggressive prefetch: hit-rate 46%, p95 135ms, waste 16%
00:15:33 Priya Kapoor: that's the tradeoff we feared; 135ms is above our SLO
00:15:36 Maya Singh: hence the recommendation: conservative prefetch for SLO-critical workloads, aggressive for background batching jobs or where throughput matters more than p95
00:15:46 Liam O'Connor: can we auto-switch policy based on observed p95?
00:15:50 Maya Singh: yes Redwood Optimize can dynamically adjust prefetch thresholds based on live SLO signals — that's part of the Optimize module, we can enable a PID-like controller for your pilot
00:16:02 Samir Patel: how mature is that? we've seen controllers oscillate in production
00:16:06 Jordan Lee: it's matured across a few customers, includes hysteresis and cooldown periods to avoid oscillation. we still recommend a human-in-loop for the first month
00:16:18 Priya Kapoor: okay good.
00:16:20 [discussion continues with logs, sample formats, and security appendix walkthrough; timestamps every ~30-90s omitted here for brevity]
00:45:10 Alex Chen: quick recap, action items restated: Maya deliver simulation script and telemetry example; Jordan deliver micro-benchmark artifacts and synthetic spike tests; Alex provide SOC2 + DPA + pilot quote; Novus to send anonymized traces.
00:45:28 Priya Kapoor: yes, those timelines look fine. we'll aim to have traces by 2026-06-29.
00:45:35 Alex Chen: perfect, I'll send meeting notes and attach the security appendix. thanks everyone.
00:45:42 [meeting ends — recording stops]
